content: Snake venom-induced consumption coagulopathy is a significant systemic effect caused by envenomation. Observational studies indicate that antivenom may improve outcomes in some cases of venom-induced consumption coagulopathy, but not in others. However, the overall effectiveness of snake antivenom in all cases of this condition remains a subject of debate. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of snake antivenom as a treatment for venom-induced consumption coagulopathy in individuals who have suffered snakebites. The search for relevant studies was conducted on January 30, 2015. Databases searched included the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library), Ovid MEDLINE(R), Ovid MEDLINE(R) In-Process & Other Non-Indexed Citations, Ovid MEDLINE(R) Daily, Ovid OLDMEDLINE(R), Embase Classic+Embase (OvidSP), as well as three additional sources, clinical trial registries, and reference lists. The selection criteria included all completed, published or unpublished, randomized controlled trials that included a placebo or no-treatment arm, where snake antivenom was administered to humans with venom-induced consumption coagulopathy following a snakebite. Two authors independently reviewed the identified trials and applied the selection criteria. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. The authors concluded that randomized placebo-controlled trials are necessary to determine the effectiveness of snake antivenom for clinically significant outcomes in patients with venom-induced consumption coagulopathy caused by snakebites. While such trials may pose ethical challenges, the routine use of a treatment with a substantial risk of anaphylaxis cannot be justified without robust evidence of its benefits.
